item.title: Things To Do in Sydney in December: A One-Day Itinerary
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
Have one day in Sydney? This itinerary takes you from sunrise at Bondi Beach to dinner on Sydney Harbour, with famous sights, Christmas shopping, and food stops along the way. It's a full day, so choose the stops that interest you most instead of trying to fit everything in. The city grew around its harbor, so the Opera House, The Rocks, the arcades, and the gardens are all close to the waterfront. If you plan well, you spend the day seeing things instead of traveling between them. Sydney in December sweetens the deal. The water is warm, the sun sets late, and the city lights up with decorated trees and market stalls. Christmas party cruises in Sydney put the harbor into the festive mood. Here's a full December itinerary, from sunrise at Bondi Beach to dinner on the harbor, packed with some of the best things to do in Sydney in December. Start where Sydney starts its mornings. Bondi is a wide curve of pale sand about 0.6 miles (1 km) long, facing east, so the sun rises straight over the sea. The water is clear and turquoise, and a Bondi Beach sunrise is worth setting an alarm for. Arrive early for a swim at Bondi Icebergs, a saltwater pool cut into the rock where waves break over the wall. Otherwise, swim between the red and yellow flags, which go out when patrols start around 8 am. Finish with breakfast on Campbell Parade, where cafes open early, and tables face the water. Bondi is about 5 miles (8 km) from the city: 30-45 minutes on the 333 bus from Circular Quay, 20 minutes by taxi. - Best for: ocean sunrise, an early swim and beachfront breakfast - Time needed: 2 to 3 hours, including travel - Cost: free for the beach, $10 for the Icebergs pool - Good to know: Thursdays are normally reserved for cleaning, though summer opening depends on tides. Check current pool hours before visiting. Circular Quay is the harbor's front door, where ferries, trains, and city streets meet. Two of Circular Quay's best-known attractions sit side by side a few minutes away. Ten minutes east of the Quay, the Royal Botanic Garden Sydney stretches along the water's edge: lawns, old fig trees, more than 27,000 plants, and curving paths with the harbor peeking through. Entry is free; it opens at 7 am, and the paths are flat. Follow the path around the point to Mrs Macquarie's Chair, a bench convicts carved into sandstone in 1810 for Elizabeth Macquarie, the governor's wife. From there, the Opera House and the Harbour Bridge line up in one frame, making it a well-liked spot to visit. - Best for: free harbor views, shade, and the best photo spot in the city - Good to know: the Chair sits at the far end of the point, so allow for the walk The garden path leads straight to it. You have seen the Sydney Opera House a thousand times in photos, and it still surprises up close: the white shells are far bigger than they look, and the surface is covered in small tiles that shift color with the light. It opened in 1973 and now carries UNESCO World Heritage status. You can walk around the forecourt and wide steps outside, and guided tours take you inside the concert halls. Walk around to the back toward the ferry wharves for a stunning view of the Harbour Bridge. - Best for: close-up views of the sails and a free harbor walk - Time needed: 30 minutes outside, 1 hour with a tour - Good to know: book the tour ahead, as popular slots go early A ten-minute walk back around the Quay takes you from the oldest part of Sydney to the middle of the modern city. The Rocks is where the city began; Martin Place is where it keeps Christmas. Between them sit lunch and the first sign of the season. Walk a few minutes west of the Quay and the streets narrow fast. The Rocks is a cluster of sandstone lanes, stairways, and courtyards below the Harbour Bridge, now filled with pubs, cafes, and galleries. The First Fleet landed here in 1788, so European settlement in Australia started on this shoreline. Of all the things to do in The Rocks Sydney, lunch in one of the country's oldest pubs comes first. Several sit within ten minutes of each other and still argue over which came first. On weekends, markets fill the streets with food and craft stalls. - Best for: colonial history, old pubs and lanes worth getting lost in - Time needed: 1.5 to 2 hours with lunch - Good to know: markets run only on weekends, so weekdays are quieter with fewer stalls. Ten minutes from The Rocks on foot, Martin Place is a long pedestrian square lined with banks, offices, and old stone buildings. In December, it becomes Sydney's Christmas centerpiece. The tree here is the tallest in New South Wales, lit by more than 110,000 lights, and the Martin Place Christmas markets fill the square below it with food, drinks and handmade gifts. - Best for: Christmas shopping, street food and the biggest tree in the state - Cost: free to walk through, stalls priced individually - Good to know: In 2026, markets run November 28 to December 24 on selected days, generally Wednesday to Saturday, with daily trading in the final week. Check the schedule before visiting. The tree lights up after dark. Afternoon - Shopping Arcades and Gardens If you still have energy, choose the Queen Victoria Building for shopping and architecture or the Chinese Garden of Friendship for a quieter break. Alternatively, return to your hotel to rest and change before taking a dinner cruise. Locals call it the QVB. Opened in 1898, the Queen Victoria Building fills a city block on George Street and features five floors of stained glass, iron railings, and a central dome under a glass ceiling. It's now a shopping center, with boutiques, jewelers, and cafes on every level, so come for the building as much as the shops. In December, an enormous Christmas tree hangs through the atrium. - Best for: shopping, Victorian architecture, and a cool break from the heat - Good to know: the upper galleries give the best view of the dome and tree. A ten-minute walk south from the QVB takes you to the southern end of Darling Harbour where a high wall hides one of the city's quietest places. The Chinese Garden of Friendship opened in 1988 and is modeled on private gardens from southern China. Inside, you'll find lakes with koi carp, waterfalls, and pavilions, while the walls block much of the traffic noise. A teahouse serves tea and dim sum. - Best for: quiet, shade, and photos unlike anything else that day - Good to know: open daily 10 am to 5 pm, with free 35-minute tours twice daily. Closed on Christmas Day. Darling Harbour is the waterfront on the city's western side. In December, the whole precinct lights up with a Christmas tree floating on Cockle Bay. For things to do in Darling Harbour at night, start with the light tunnel, then board a dinner cruise. A few minutes from the water, Darling Square sets up a light tunnel each December, lit every night until Christmas. The lights arch over the path so you can walk the whole length and stop for photos. More than 50 places to eat and drink line it, making it a great spot as the sun drops toward the horizon. - Best for: Christmas lights, waterfront bars and a sunset walk - Good to know: time it for dusk, when the tunnel shows up best End the day aboard one of the Sydney dinner cruises, departing from King Street Wharf a few minutes from Darling Square. This is the signature Sydney way to wrap up an evening: dinner and a live show on a boat cruising Sydney Harbour. Christmas versions run through December and are ideal for groups. - Best for: a signature Sydney dinner cruise with live cabaret - Time needed: around 3 hours on the water - Cost: ticketed, with dinner and the show included - Good to know: book ahead, as December evenings fill early That's a full day in Sydney, from first light at Bondi to an evening on the harbor. Skip a stop or two for a slower pace, and leave enough time to reach King Street Wharf before your cruise's boarding time. This article was published in partnership with Sydney Showboats.

item.title: A lakeside idyll: laid-back cycling and autumn hikes on Italy’s Lake Iseo
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
Rust red and burnt sienna speckle the green mountain rising from Lake Iseo. Golden autumn sunlight shimmers on the water. Monte Isola, Italyâs largest lake island, is a peak of sheer cliffs and dense forest, dotted with old fishing hamlets and hillside villages, each as pretty as the terraced villas of Lake Como and Garda, but with far fewer visitors. I arrive at the small port town of Peschiera Maraglio â where striped wooden boats jut from the water like the gondolas of Venice â on a ferry from Sulzano, a five-minute hop across the water. âOnly three people on the island are allowed to own a car: the priest, the doctor and the mayor,â says Chiara, my tour guide from Brescia. Residents can zip up and down the steep island roads on mopeds, and a small fleet of van-sized buses trundle around throughout the day, but nearly all cars are forbidden and visitors have to explore on foot or bike. Even bikes are banned from boats at the weekend. Not that it matters: the harbour front is lined with bike rentals (from â¬4 an hour for a standard bike). Iâm normally a nervous cyclist, but car-free roads raise my confidence. Plus, most other visitors have the telltale front-wheel wobble of novice riders. This isnât the place for Lycra and personal bests; the smooth-as-silk, quiet roads are for slow pedalling, and neck swivelling to take in another gorgeous view of Lake Iseo. The circular lakeside route winds past olive groves tumbling to the shore. I thought Iâd need base layers and gloves this far into autumn, but Iâm in shorts and a T-shirt and already working up a sweat in 24C sunshine. I pedal through the lakeside hamlet of Sensole in the islandâs south-west and stop in Menzino, just along the shore. Thereâs a cafe-bar catering to cyclists, so I fuel up with an espresso con lake view. The view from the western side of the island is somewhat marred by a huge concrete factory on the mainland, so I keep my head down on the pedal to Siviano, the islandâs capital. The shambling streets are sleepy; the stacked skyline of orange, lemon and magnolia villas is punctuated by the looming facade of Santi Faustino e Giovita church and a medieval stone tower. Monte Isola has been inhabited since the Roman era. Venetian rule in the 15th and 16th centuries left the main towns resembling those on Garda and Como: hillside terraces of wooden-shuttered pastel villas. In the late 18th century, Monte Isola found its main industry: net making. At Retificio La Rete Srl, a small shop and net factory at Sivianoâs port, fishing nets have been handwoven for centuries, along with nets for basketball hoops, football goals, shopping bags and hammocks. At the northern tip of the island, I get the best views of Lake Iseoâs craggiest mountains. The south of the lake is chalk-white bell towers against gently undulating hills, draped in franciacorta vineyards. The north is where jagged peaks scrape the sky, plummeting to the emerald-green lake water. Just off the shore, a speck of an island (Isola di Loreto) is topped with a grand, castle-like building, which Chiara says is privately owned. A flotilla of kayakers from Marone make their way towards the private dock, slipping across the glass-still water. In Carzano, I pause to admire thepink-and-white facade of San Giovanni Battista church, before cycling along the more functional stretch of road along the eastern shore. The traffic-free spell is broken by an old Fiat Punto, apologetically crawling along the road. Maybe the driver is the doctor or priest. I complete my circle back in Peschiera Maraglio, where a late lunch of lake fish awaits at La Foresta restaurant. To begin, pickled tench so vinegary it makes my mouth water and a chub carpaccio that tastes like fresh lake water; followed by the island staple of dried, salted sardinas on grilled polenta. âSardina is not a sardine; itâs actually a type of shad fish,â Chiara explains. âIn the middle ages, when Monte Isola had to pay tax to Venice, they didnât understand how money worked, so they paid in salted sardinas instead.â As the last ferries leave for the evening, it feels as if I have Peschiera Maraglio to myself. Accommodation is private holiday apartments or restaurants with rooms. At Decio, a modern bistro dominates the ground floor, with a handful of sleek bedrooms above. The glass front shows off an uninterrupted lake view and the room is bathed in orange light at sunset. I spend the evening perched on a stool outside LâIsola dei Sapori, a no-frills alfresco spot where sparkling franciacorta wine is perfectly chilled, and snacks of local salami, olives and fish dishes combine for a light dinner. The next day, I forgo my bike and lace up my hiking boots. The steep trail to the top of the island begins with the enclosed cobbled streets of Peschiera Maraglio and wends into thick chestnut forest. I pocket a particularly beefy conker, unable to resist the childhood urge for a blinder. My legs start to burn against the gradient â the trail is 450 metres of climbing. Rocks and twisting roots burst through the forest path and thereâs a sheer drop to one side, but the glimpses of Lake Iseo between the trees are worth every wheeze. After an hour, the trees thin out and I emerge at Santuario della Madonna della Ceriola. The striking white sanctuary was built in the 13th century, on the remains of a pagan temple and early Christian chapels. A vast golden altar and detailed frescoes adorn the interior, but itâs the panoramic view outside that really makes the hike worthwhile. The ferry to Sulzano is a toy boat, leaving a white tail of wake. From up high, I see that autumn colours are already creeping into the forest. I wipe the sweat from my eyes. This view is only going to get prettier as the season evolves, and the prize conkers are yet to fall. The trip was arranged by Visit Brescia. Bike rental starts at â¬4 an hour. The ferry from Sulzano to Monte Isola is â¬2.60 each way. Trains run from Brescia to Sulzano from â¬4.10. Rooms at Decio start at â¬90 B&B

item.title: ‘A winning combination of culture and nature’: exploring Germany’s green heart by bus
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
Itâs early morning in Erfurt, the capital of Germanyâs Thuringia region, and Domplatz is abuzz with local growers setting out crates of vegetables and flowers beneath the soaring medieval cathedral towers. This 14th- and 15th-century engineering wonder holds the Gloriosa, the worldâs largest medieval free-swinging bell, cast in 1497 and weighing 12 tonnes. Though the city and surrounding landscape are notably flat, its skyline is pierced by soaring church towers and steeples, the atmospheric old town hardly changed over the centuries. Thuringia â often called the âgreen heart of Germanyâ â lies in the centre of the country, between Hesse, Saxony and Bavaria. Itâs famous for its dense forests, intellectual heritage and hearty cuisine, and Iâm here for four days to explore using public transport. Leaving Frankfurt behind, my three-hour coach journey rolls through rising forested highlands before descending into the wide, agricultural basin that cradles Erfurt. After checking out Domplatzâs morning market, itâs just a short walk to one of the townâs other famous sights, the 120-metre-long KrÃ¤merbrÃ¼cke â a 14th-century bridge lined with colourful half-timbered houses. Erfurt was once at the crossroads of two major trade routes, and the wealth that built its impressive churches and merchantsâ houses came partly from waid, or woad, a plant cultivated in the surrounding fields and processed for its blue dye. I stroll past the craft shops (some still sell the dye) to Petersberg Citadel, one of the largest and best-preserved fortresses in Europe, with a maze of underground tunnels. This is also the city where the Protestant Reformation took root â Martin Luther studied here and was a monk in the Augustinian monastery (you can join a guided tour or even stay overnight). Dinner is in a suitably historic setting; Wirtshaus Christoffel, in the Haus zur weiÃen Lilie (House of the White Lily), dates back to the 12th century (the house-brewed beer and beef roulade with Thuringian dumplings are delicious). Next morning, I head to Egapark (a seven-minute bus ride or a 30-minute walk from town). Spread across 36 hectares (89 acres), it was created for the 1961 international horticultural exhibition. The old Cyriaksburg fortress houses the German Horticultural Museum, which traces the history of gardening, while displays range from landscapes of cacti and succulents to tropical planting. The city of Weimar, a 30-minute bus journey away, is next on my list. The birthplace of the artistic Bauhaus movement, and where Germanyâs first democratic constitution was adopted, itâs full of interesting historic sites and design gems. I visit the Bauhaus museum, with its ceramics, textiles, metalwork and painting, and wander around town, passing the former art school buildings that now house the Bauhaus-UniversitÃ¤t. The next morning, I swap culture for chilling and take another bus to Bad Langensalza, a spa town of 10 parks and themed gardens, 40 miles (64km) away. My guide, Markus Fromm, explains that people come here to âcure, to relax, to refreshâ. Sulphur springs were discovered here in 1811, and today, the Friederiken Therme is the townâs main thermal spa, offering natural sulphur, brine and drinking mineral waters, alongside indoor and outdoor pools, saunas and treatments. Traces of the older spa history remain around the town: at FriederikenschlÃ¶sschen, an 18th-century summer residence, a fountain still runs with sulphur water that has been used for healing since 1812. But itâs the townâs gardens that really win me over. I wander FriederikenschlÃ¶sschenâs restored baroque garden and visit the Klagetor, a gate tower dating from about 1365, where the old town gives way to the Japanese garden, Kofuku no Niwa (Garden of Happiness), with its koi ponds, clipped azaleas and sculpted pines. For nature on an even grander scale, I take a bus to Hainich national park, 10 minutes away (you can easily rent a bike/e-bike and follow cycling paths to get there too). Spanning 7,500 hectares, Hainich offers more than 75 miles of signposted walking trails through its beech forests, part of a Unesco world heritage site. The wider Hainich is Germanyâs largest unbroken deciduous woodland area. âParts of this landscape have been left entirely untouched for decades, abandoned to their own devices without a shred of human meddling,â says park director RÃ¼diger Biehl. Before hitting the trail, I stop at the parkâs restaurant, Forsthaus Thiemsburg, for a regional lunch â roast pork in black beer and Thuringian dumplings, washed down with a cold KÃ¶stritzer pilsner. Then, into the trees. Deep in the beeches, the sun sporadically breaks through the branches and the leaves crunch loudly under my boots. Up in the canopy, itâs mostly just the birds making noise â chaffinches and wood warblers chatter, interrupted by the occasional sharp rattle of a middle spotted woodpecker drilling into a trunk. The Baumkronenpfad, a wooden walkway through the treetops, rises to a 44-metre observation tower. Here, the canopy of an oak that is estimated to be 350 years old is almost at eye level. Itâs a spectacular view, but the forestâs real engine is down below. Deadwood is left to decay where it falls, providing habitat for rare wood-boring insects and endangered Bechsteinâs bats. Back in Erfurt that evening, I catch the final symphony concert of the season at Theaterplatz. Itâs a reminder of the winning combination of culture and nature that Iâve enjoyed over my four days in Thuringia. I had come looking for a less familiar corner of Germany and found a region that offers plenty of variety â and all accessible with a few short bus rides. The trip was provided by the German National Tourist Board. Dorint Hotel am Dom in Erfurt has doubles from Â£85. For journey planning, VMT has information on buses, trains and trams across central Thuringia, as well as a free app with live departure updates

item.title: Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
I havenât made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what Iâd make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if youâre lucky, theyâre also stuffed with a nutty cheese)âthis style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casingâs texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid. Need to make a substitution? - Step 1Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6â8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1â1Â½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate. Step 2Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and Â½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Â¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6â8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute. Step 3Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1Â½ cups apple cider, 1Â½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, Â½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining Â½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Â¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30â35 minutes. Step 4Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

item.title: Ever wondered where Halloween was born? Let us take you back 2,000 years to Ireland's eerie ‘Hell Cave’
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
As Irish folklore tells, a black horse with glowing eyes sprints through the Emerald Isle's raw countryside in the murky night, carrying a terrified countryman who canât escape this ghastly ride. They gallop past eerie sites, which have now become tourist attractions â mystical fairy forts, prehistoric passage tombs, abandoned Royal capitals, and the âhell caveâ where Halloween was born. While Halloween was popularised by the US in the 1900s, the holiday originated 2,000 years ago with Irelandâs pagan festival, Samhain. Now, Ireland is making moves to reclaim the celebrations, branding itself as the world capital of Halloween. An island-wide tourism campaign involving dozens of events, including fire processions, carnival parades, and Europeâs biggest Halloween festival has launched this month, in a bid to bring the holiday back to its original setting. Each event is designed around helping tell the creepy history of Samhain, during which supernatural beings ran riot across Ireland. Inhabited for up 10,000 years, Irelandâs green fields, serene forests and raw coastline echo with riveting folklore. The Irish people respect the Celtic mythology, telling stories of these beings, like the aforementioned Puca horse. Some such tales are mere campfire stories, describing lost cities and invisible islands. Others are grounded in reality, like that of Samhain. Every November 1, on Samhain, Irish pagans would mark the Celtic New Year by chanting alongside bonfires at sacred sites such as Oweynagat hell cave â a supposed portal to Irelandâs mythical underworld, TÃr na nÃg. This subterranean realm bulges with Sidhe fairies, including leprechauns and pucas, which are infamous for supposedly abducting humans after dark. Sidhes are trapped in TÃr na nÃg, which is supposedly separated from the living world by an invisible border. Every now and then, this barrier briefly dissolves. Sidhes emerge from the underworld to either save the Irish people or plunge them into disasters, like the Great Irish Famine, according to mythology. Samhain is the main moment this spirit invasion occurred. During the early versions of this festival, Sidhes would pour out of Oweynagat cave and swarm adjoining Rathcroghan, the capital of Irelandâs ancient kingdom of Connachta. Meanwhile, Samhainâs human attendees prayed for protection from fairies, in between feasting, dancing and trading at Rathcroghan. Now known as Europeâs largest un-excavated royal complex, Rathcroghan allows visitors to wander fields dotted by its 240 archaeological sites, including stone forts and ceremonial mounds. Tourists keen to known how Samhain inspired Halloween can join guided tours of Rathcroghan and Oweynagat, or they may attend the nearby Rathcroghan Visitor Centre, which has a small but informative museum. There they learn that, in the 1800s, Irish immigrants brought Samhain to the US, where it gradually became a kitschy, commercialised festival aimed at children. Which explains why Ireland last year decided to plant its flag on this festival by launching its annual âHome of Halloweenâ programme, says Julie Wakley, head of Great Britain for Tourism Ireland. "Halloween is one of the most widely celebrated festivals globally, yet many people are surprised to discover that its roots trace back to the island of Ireland,â Wakley explains. Home of Halloween involves dozens of events across the entire island of Ireland â festivals, performances, food experiences, walking tours â and is a collaboration between Tourism Ireland and Tourism Northern Ireland. Northern Ireland is home to plenty of spooky places itself â including the Dark Hedges, a lane of overhanging beech trees, often used as a filming location in series such as The Game of Thrones. Puca Festival (October 29 to November 1) in County Meathâs Boyne Valley incorporates heritage tours, live music events, a mythical character parade and a stunning fire procession that mirrors prehistoric Samhain rituals. Northern Irelandâs Derry Halloween (October 28 to November 1) is Europeâs largest Halloween festival, with events focused on storytelling, music, dance, fire shows, and a replica of an ancient Samhain harvest market. Meanwhile, smaller Halloween festivals will unfurl in the cities of Dublin, Limerick, Galway, Longford and Kilkenny. Each of Irelandâs Halloween festivals is slightly different in character. But all have one thing in common: they aim to remind the world that, eons before sinister-looking pumpkins were carved by US kids, this festival was being celebrated by chanting, costumed Irish Pagans illuminated by bonfires. Ireland is reclaiming Halloween. Irelandâs spooky sites to visit for Halloween Some 2,000 years ago, Irish pagans accessed this âhell caveâ through a purpose-built entrance. Now, thereâs only a narrow opening in a tranquil field, 140km west of Dublin. Tourists can peek into its dim interior, or read a nearby sign explaining its extraordinary history. But theyâre not allowed to squeeze inside the cave, for safety reasons. No ticket is required. Grassy mounds rising from farmland contain remains of this Irish Royal capital, some 5,500 years old, which hosted ancient Samhain celebrations. During those rituals, shapeshifting beasts escaped from Irelandâs underworld to haunt Rathcroghanâs 6.5sqkm of forts, earthworks and standing stones. Visitors can access Rathcroghan at any time, for free. But itâs worth booking a 2.5 hour guided tour via nearby Rathcroghan Visitor Centre, for â¬21.20. Rathcroghan Visitor Centre, County Roscommon Located in tiny Tulsk town, 4km east of Rathcroghan, it has a cafÃ©, gift shop, and petite museum. That latter facility, which costs â¬6 to enter, explains Rathcroghanâs ties to Samhain and Irelandâs eerie underworld, and displays ancient artefacts from this site. It is open year-round, Monday to Saturday, from 9.15am to 5pm. Sligoâs mountainous countryside contains more than 100 eerie "passage tombs" up to 5,000 years old, including at scenic Carrowkeel and Carrowmore. It remains unclear whoâs buried inside the majority of these stone tombs, the most spectacular of which is Keshcorran, overlooking majestic countryside. Local lore suggests Keshcorranâs tunnels are connected, underground, to Oweynagat "hell caveâ. Entry is free, at all times, and itâs a moderate 15-minute uphill walk from the carpark. National Leprechaun Museum of Ireland, County Dublin Rather than providing a cartoonish explanation of leprechauns, this museum in downtown Dublin unravels the Irish folklore ofÂ Sidhe fairies. Visitors must join guided tours, which mix eyecatching video displays depicting Irish artefacts and ancient maps, with storytelling about Irelandâs supernatural beings. These 45-minute tours depart every 30 minutes, and cost â¬18 per adult. Cnoc Meadha Fairy Fortress, County Galway A dense, serene forest provides fine protection for Cnoc Meadha, the underground fortress supposedly home to Ireland's Sidhe fairies, who were key characters in Samhain lore. Visitors can take a scenic, 10-minute uphill walk from the carpark to reach this 1,000-year-old site, the legendary headquarters of the King of the Sidhes, Finvarra. During ancient Samhain celebrations, bonfires glowed so intensely atop this 3,000-year-old ceremonial site that it was named Tlachtga, after a Celtic goddess of the sun. Now commonly called the Hill of Ward, it sits on private farmland in County Meath. But tourists can access it by joining one of the daily 90-minute Hill of Ward guided tours between October 29 and November 1, for â¬27.50 per adult. Blood stained the Hill of Ward during prehistoric Samhain rituals, which saw animals sacrificed to Pagan demons. This prehistoric Royal burial site, in emerald fields 18km east of Tlachtga, is now a heritage attraction, with free access to visitors seven days a week.

item.title: Megan Thee Stallion Revealed Her Favorite Glute Exercise—Donkey Kicks. A Personal Trainer Says Hikers Can Do Them As a Warm-Up.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
The donkey kick exercise isn’t new: this move is a longtime staple in Pilates, barre, and bodyweight workouts. But it is newly trendy, thanks to Megan Thee Stallion shouting out the donkey kick as one of her go-to exercises in a recent interview with The Cut. “I’m going to call them stallion kicks,” the Grammy Award-winning rapper joked in the interview. What’s much less funny, though, is how much this exercise can fire up, and burn out, your glutes. As a certified personal trainer, I’ve programmed this move into my own workouts and into group fitness classes, too, because it’s a really effective way to isolate your butt muscles. Here’s why the donkey kick is so good for your glutes. And doing them regularly can keep your lower body ready so you can take on the trails with ease. The starting position for the donkey kick is really simple. First, get on all fours with your wrists under your shoulders and knees under your hips. From there, lift one leg straight up, keeping the knee on that same lifted leg bent to 90 degrees. Then, with control, lower your leg back down to complete one rep. Do a set number of reps; you can do the standard ten reps if you’d like, but if you want to bang out more, then that’s totally OK. Then switch legs and do ten on that leg. That’s one set. Repeat for three sets. This move looks pretty easy, and in a sense, it is. Many other lower-body exercises that work the glutes—like squats, lunges, step-ups, and deadlifts—also engage other muscle groups. But because the donkey kick keeps your knees bent, which largely takes your hamstrings out of the equation, you’re really just isolating your glutes here. That means it hits those muscles—hard. The gluteus maximus (your biggest butt muscle) does the heavy lifting to raise your elevated leg, while your gluteus medius and minimus (two smaller muscles that form your side butt) help stabilize your hips. Your core also stabilizes the move, and an engaged core keeps your torso still while you move one leg at a time. You’ll know you’re doing the move correctly when you feel lots of tension in your butt. Though it’s a great way to isolate your glutes, donkey kicks do have their limitations. For one, they’re not the most functional—meaning the exercise doesn’t closely resemble how we typically move in sports or day-to-day life. Contrast that with a step-up, squat, or lunge, which also work the glutes but in more typical movement patterns similar to how you’d hike up or downhill. Second, it’s hard to add a bunch of external load to the donkey kick. Sure, you could place a dumbbell under the knee of your lifted leg, or loop a resistance band above your knees (or even wear ankle weights), but you can’t easily pile on a ton of external load. The end result? You eventually reach a ceiling with your glute-strengthening gains. If you’re a hiker, runner, or backpacker, the donkey kick can have a time and place in your workout routine. As the International Sports Sciences Association points out, incorporating this exercise into a warm-up can help you activate your glutes more effectively during the rest of your workout. That’s exactly how I’d program them for outdoor athletes: do them before your next hike, run, or backpacking adventure to switch on your glutes so your butt is ready to work as soon as you hit the trail. When your glutes are fired up and ready before your favorite outdoor activity, you’ll be better able to push forward with each step and may reduce your risk of knee pain and injury. Plus, the donkey kicks give you a little stretch in your hip flexors—muscles that are chronically tight in many people—so loosening them up can help you more comfortably navigate terrain. item.title: This Cookbook Author Explores Cemeteries for Recipes To Die For
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
A recipe quite literally taken to the grave? Thatâs the foundation for creator Rosie Grantâs ongoing archival project turned cookbook To Die For. And itâs exactly how it sounds. Apropos for Spooky Season, the book collects âgravestone recipesâ so synonymous with departed loved ones theyâre immortalized on their headstones. It celebrates the legacies of ordinary folks who did extraordinary things. They were teachers or coaches, the local dentist, the neighbor everybody knew, and they all showed love through cooking for their communities. What began as a light curiosity turned into a larger, more emotional realization around identity, place, and what we leave behind. Over the past five and a half years since starting her TikTok and Instagram accounts under the username ghostly.archive during a digital archives internship at the Congressional Cemetery in Washington, DC, Grantâs travels have taken her across the United Statesâas far as Nome, Alaskaâas well as Nova Scotia, to visit their final resting places and families to learn their stories. To Die For features many baked goods that yield dozens per batch, evoking comforting funeral foods. Cookies and cakes adapting mostly traditional Americana nostalgia (spritz cookies, brownies, carrot cake) appear alongside more surprising inclusions like a WWIIâera guava cobbler; glazed, no-bake blueberry pie; and the little-known true story behind the beloved Irish coffee. Other recipes list ingredients for a Jack Danielâs marinade, easy cheese and ranch dips, rustic breads, and savories like meatloaf (âTexasâ best,â per the engraving), fried ripe tomato, spaghetti chicken casserole and kasha varnishkes, to name a few. Itâs an almost feel-good way to get into the topics of mortality and death, Grant assesses, as sitting around the table to share a meal or stepping into a memory-filled kitchen disintegrates conversational barriers. Though she was raised by parents who gave ghost tours at local cemeteries in Alexandria, Virginia, she says her family was much more comfortable with the idea of hauntings than discussing and planning for the inevitable themselves. âSomething like a recipe feels so life-giving,â Grant expresses, adding that these conversations could also encompass music or travel. âTalking about these many life-filling moments might be an easier way to talk about tough topics.â The 40 recipes were all approved by family members of the deceased, whom Grant tracked down mostly through internet sleuthing (obituaries and social media) to ask permission to publish. Richard Dawson and his daughter, Nailah, set the tone for the book when Grant met them two years after she first found out about Dawsonâs mother. Naomi Odessa Miller-Dawsonâs headstone is outfitted with a recipe book open to her famous spritz cookies atop her epitaph in Brooklynâs Green-Wood Cemetery. Her fierce but quiet passion for baking has been exalted by the family since her passing in 2009, making Naomiâs one of the most well-known gravestone recipes in country through online chats and Reddit threads. Initially Grant tried to separate the recipe from its provider and solely focus on the food itself, but the process didnât feel quite right. âThe way Richard talked about waiting by the oven for the cookies to come out, recalling smells from when he was a little kid, trying to eat them right off the tray even though itâs still a little hot,â Grant recalls. âIt really changed the project in the sense that it made the project.â Grant has since cooked with seven families highlighted in To Die For, and has shared her pilgrimages to the gravesites with the goods themselves to pay respect. With her years of research and immersion, Grant notes that burials and grave markers have become so much more personal over the course of time. Granite headstones have allowed for almost any customization after mass-industrialization made the tools to work on it more accessible, and are much more durable compared to the formerly used wood, slate, or marble, making for lasting memorials. Proof cemeteries are beautiful grounds still vibrating with life and knowledge, if youâre open to it. Her approach to keeping such individual histories alive has deeply resonated, furthering her relationship to the Death Positive Movement: formed by hospice workers, death doulas and other care workers who advocate that discussions around mortality and afterlife planning make for a healthier society; and establishing a more intimate sense of collectivity amongst strangers across the globe. While sheâs gotten her share of detractors for various reasons (mainly self-identified Mediums claiming the deceased, and in one caseâone participant still living, didnât appreciate their culinary secrets being shared), many folks have found inspiration as they consider their own gravestone recipe. Some commenters, meanwhile, express regret around not asking their own loved ones for recipes or helpful tips that most instructions donât leave nuance for when they had the chance. âI thought I could just have this on socials and do a PDF format online,â Grant says. â[The families] were like âWe like the idea of a physical book. Something thatâs precious.â Even the visual style of it is meant to be something youâd inherit from a grandparent.â The most underrated section of her book offers a thoughtful list of questions to begin documenting oneâs own familial food legacies. âIt can feel really morbid to be like âHey mom, can you write down your recipe because youâre gonna die someday?ââ Grant says jokingly. âThat can look like a lot things. Take pictures of the recipe box and text it to all the cousins or the family group chat and save it to a drive somewhere. Cook with your family member. Teach me how to do it, letâs cook it together. Passing down that knowledge, thereâs something very powerful about that shared experience.â Sentiments from both participants in the book and Grantâs audience echo how revisiting these recipes offers sensory catharsis in addition to talking about their grief. What started as a nerdy food adventure manifested into an exploration of what it means to be remembered for how people made us feel when we were with them; highlighting turn-of-the-century attitudes toward heritage, family and home life, and serving as a ârite of passageâ or way to pass the torch to the next generation. Grant reminds us of observing and maintaining such rituals. âIf we donât do it, nobody else will.â

item.title: The man hiking the world in search of rare cheeses
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
The man hiking the world in search of rare cheeses Trevor Warmedahl has spent years documenting rare and traditional cheesemaking methods, and believes that "cheese is an edible manifestation of a place". Trevor Warmedahl was working as a commercial cheesemaker in Seattle when he realised he was using milk that came from animals he never saw. So, he quit his job and set off on what has become a global odyssey to discover places that still make cheese the old-fashioned way. In 2019 he arrived in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, and lived alone in a yurt with a dog as his companion. He soon discovered that dairy was sacred there: the women flicked milk into the air before cheesemaking, a gesture of respect called a milk libation. He visited homes where whey bubbled over central hearths and fresh, unripened byaslag cheese covered tables. After hiking to shrines, he noticed people offered dairy products as a symbol of purity. As summer unfolded and city-dwellers migrated to the Mongolian steppe to farm, Warmedahl itched to join. He jumped on a Soviet-era coal-powered sleeper train for a rickety overnight ride across the Gobi Desert. On the journey back to Ulaanbaatar, he met a local who invited him to stay with her herder family on the Zavkhan grassland. Warmedahl spent that summer waking before dawn to milk yaks, chasing livestock up the valley on horses, listening to shepherds' folk songs at sunset and cooking milk into dehydrated, sweet-and-sour curds called aaruul. The experience inspired him to seek out other places preserving rare cheesemaking traditions before they disappeared. During the past six years, Warmedahl has hitched, hiked and driven through more than 20 countries, documenting traditional cheesemaking and pastoral lifestyles, and offering workshops on natural dairy processing. After recently completing a 193km (120-mile) cheese trek across the Peaks of the Balkans Trail, he shared with the BBC what cheesemaking reveals about a place. Ancestral cheeses in Georgia have no analogues – I call them "fossil cheeses" because they were almost lost but are making a comeback as part of a broader post-Soviet cultural revival. My pinnacle moment happened in Tusheti, a mountain region bordering Russia near the tourist village of Omalo. I showed up with vague directions to the shepherds' summer camp, which was deep in the valley. That's a theme: the cheeses I find are always far out, made by hermit types sticking to the old ways out of sheer stubbornness. It was drop-dead gorgeous, just me and my backpack. The valley ends on an abrupt cliff, with deteriorating medieval stone towers. Shepherds build their camps from the decay. I saw how these guys milked sheep by hand with wooden pails, rustic-style. It's a feta-like cheese called Tushuri guda, aged in inside-out sheepskins. At the end of the season, I walked about 130km (81 miles) back down the valley with them and 300 sheep. The herd has done this for generations – they know where to go. The shepherds just coordinated, and it created this crazy lawless feeling with dogs barking and me, chasing stray sheep down ravines. At night we'd build a campfire and drink, and even with the language barrier, we'd relate through food. Sometimes language isn't needed. In cheesemaking, if two hearts want to connect, they'll find a way. How is cheese and cheesemaking a reflection of a community's history and culture? Cheese is a sensory experience and embodies larger ideas about how we live. It represents how meaningful human cultures can be. At its best, cheese reflects this complex relationship between humans, landscapes, microbial life and livestock at a time [when] we've become so separate from how food is made. And the cultural element holds the constellation together. The cheeses I highlight represent an older mentality, with a sense of stewardship over the places we live and farm. So, a little bit more of the wildness of nature slips into the product. [Cheese is] an edible manifestation of place, of cultural history transformed into delicious food. Why is cheesemaking especially important today? The diversity and range of cheese is infinite. When animals eat, they transform grass and entire landscapes into milk that becomes cheese, and animals can graze [almost] anywhere. So, it's a lifestyle that can move in response to climate uncertainty and desertification – real challenges today. The cheeses I focus on – natural farmstead cheeses [made exclusively with milk from a farmer's own animals] – reflect deep, ethical relationships between people and livestock and highlight the incredible diversity of heritage livestock. With industrialisation, that diversity is vanishing at an alarming rate. So pastoral cheesemaking strikes me as profoundly sustainable. What can so-called "exotic cheeses" that challenge us reveal about a place? There's this greyish-brown cheese from Norway, gammelost, [covered in] moulds like fruit rot. It tastes like a musty cellar with bold, mouth-numbing spiciness. It wasn't for me. But deliciousness is cultural. It's taught. So, I always say: don't try something once, try it 10 times. Uncomfortable foods open doors. But be sure to eat them because you're interested in the culture, not because they're freaky to you. One of the easiest ways to express interest in a culture is to say: feed me what you eat. When people realise you're genuine, the relationship deepens and you begin to understand their history through food. Funky cheeses become cultural emblems because of how obscure and special they are. You set out on your global cheese journey without a real plan. What did this approach add to your experience? Back then [in 2019], I was hopping on a whim from one volunteer gig to the next, drawn to remote places where people worked to protect and revitalise traditional cheeses. Workaway on farms, or staying for a while at guesthouses where cheese is made, are still amazing ways to go beyond tourism to see how people really live. Cheese gives you access to a global community, like at [the Slow Food Cheese Festival in] Bra, Italy. But anything you can do to find that deeper experience – food, handicrafts – is worth it, even if you can't always plan in advance. If your heart is in the right place and you jump fully into adventure when it calls, the details will almost always work themselves out. What advice would you give fellow travellers about how to best experience unique cheeses abroad? Find the cheese shop or cheesemonger that has the most local tilt and ask them which cheesemakers you can and should visit. Organising it yourself is cheaper. But there are also paid tours where you can experience a range of cheeses in a short period and really get to know a place. Just make sure that the cost actually supports local producers – that's what I call responsible "lacto-culinary" tourism. How can other travellers seek out responsible agrotourism experiences? Look for local cheesemakers and guides. It's also important to not expect farmers to sanitise things. It's normal to go to a farm and see broken-down equipment and mud. When we romanticise tradition, it encourages locals to put themselves in a museum. But tools [and] tradition have always evolved. More like this: We need to be open to the fact that it's not all grandmas spinning wool on wheels outside stone cottages. Then it becomes kind of a show, and we're pushing farmers to become something they're not for tourists. What places have exciting, overlooked, or under-the-radar cheeses? Where are you keen to travel next? Hands down, Turkey. It's a universe of cheese that doesn't get enough attention. Tulum peyniri is emblematic of pastoral lifestyles and the extreme sacrifice at the root of dairying and – I'd argue – life. That's because it's aged mainly in furry goatskins, so it looks insane because it can take on animal shapes. Somehow, I didn't think it would be delicious. How good can goatskin-aged cheese be, right? It was phenomenal. I was blown away by deep flavours and textures I'd never seen in cheese before. Turkish cheese needs to be talked about alongside Western Europe. More remote places have just as many fascinating cheeses to preserve and celebrate.
