item.title: Let This Dinner Menu Take You to Sicily, No Passport Needed
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine
I’m dreaming of Sicily: the land, the sea, the food, the history. The olive trees, the grapevines, the wheat fields. The wild fennel and artichokes. The market stalls piled high with just-picked cauliflower, shiny fat eggplant and cucuzzi, the yard-long summer squash that’s grown on trellises. The fish on view at the lively pescheria: swordfish, tuna and branzino, sardines, cuttlefish and urchins. This dream is making me hungry. On a recent visit to Sicily, friends from Catania took us to a small seaside restaurant with an all-fish menu. At the entrance was a small display of the day’s offerings on ice. You choose your fish before heading outside, where well-weathered, sun-bleached tables and chairs sit right on the docks. For the main course, your chosen fish is roasted whole in a wood-burning oven and then deboned. It can be served plain, with olive oil and lemon. Or it can be tossed with pasta and a quickly made sauce — that was my favorite. Recipe: Sicilian-Style Pasta With Fish Ragù The pasta was paccheri, the sturdy, pleasantly chewy shape known for its sauce-clinging nature. (You could substitute similarly hearty rigatoni, calamarata or pappardelle, if preferred.) The sauce was revelatory. It was essentially a deft ragù di pesce, a rapid sauté of onions and red peppers in olive oil, with chopped tomato and a splash of white wine. The boneless roasted fish pieces were then added. The simple combination was perfectly delicious, just saucy enough to dress the pasta. I fantasized about making it in my own kitchen. In Sicily, it was made with orata, sea bream. Back home in the States, we tried it with cod and with halibut and were more than happy with both. But nearly any firm-fleshed fish could stand in — rockfish, sea bass, corvina — whatever is spanking fresh. Instead of sitting down for the first course, we stood, nibbling on crostini topped with savory caponata, enjoyed with a bottle of crisp white Grillo. Recipe: Zucchini-Eggplant Caponata Toasts Traditional caponata is made with eggplant fried in olive oil and then simmered in a sweet-sour sauce that includes tomatoes, vinegar and sugar, along with capers, green olives, celery and sometimes raisins. There are other versions of caponata, too, made with artichokes or other seasonal vegetables, the agrodolce sauce being the through line. I made mine with zucchini and eggplant; both looked good at the market. My version is light on tomato, possibly because that’s the way I first knew it, when we used to buy it in those flat glass jars at the Italian deli. Though you can eat it right away, of course, caponata is best when it’s allowed to meld its flavors for a day or two. And since it keeps well, it’s nice to have a batch on hand in the fridge, ready at any moment to serve with drinks or as a midnight snack. Lately, for dessert, I have been enamored with roasted fruit, so I continued the theme for this meal, this time with pears, flavored with a little powdered fennel seed. They were anointed with a creamy zabaglione, kissed with Marsala, the fortified sweet wine. Sicilian zabaglione is nothing more than Marsala, egg yolks and sugar, heated and whipped into a frothy custard. In restaurants, they make a show of it, the chef in plain sight, beating the mixture vigorously by hand in a copper pan. Be warned: When making it at home, you’ll need a strong arm (or a volunteer) for all that whisking, but, for a sauce this good, it’s worth the workout.

item.title: Getting Lost in Bolivia's Wine Lands, Storied Mines, and Haunting Salt Flats
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
It is never really about the wine tasting. The balance of those subtle notes of blackberry with a finish of vanilla and leather is secondary. Wine is about landscapes and places. It is about culture and stories and the rich cast of characters: impassioned eccentrics and erudite enologists, enthusiastic amateurs and old landed families, their histories as convoluted as soap operas. Bolivian wines may not feature in many global wine shops, but in Bolivia, as is often the case, vineyards lead to some of the most interesting people in the country. I had come to the windswept altiplano in Bolivia's southwest corner, between the eastern and western cordilleras of the Andes. This vast and bleakly beautiful plateau tips away toward snow-capped mountains and empty reaches of sky. There are cactus-strewn badlands and arid highlands of lava flows; there are gulches and canyons with strange rock formations. I wanted to visit PotosÃ, one of the oldest colonial cities in the Americas, and to see the astonishing Salar de Uyuni, where new lodges have transformed the tourist experience of the salt flats. But first I wanted to drop down into the narrow fertile valleys that cut unexpectedly through the altiplano and find the winemakers around the old towns of Tarija and Tupiza, a region that surely made the first conquistadors homesick for Andalusia due to its haunting resemblance to southern Spain. If there is a Wild West feeling to Bolivian towns, with those sleepy squares of flat-fronted buildings where men, their hats tipped over their eyes, doze on chairs tilted back against walls, it may explain the country's appeal to revolutionaries and runaways, to exiles and outlaws. Che Guevara was killed here in the 1960s trying to foment revolution among Bolivian peasants. Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid were drawn here in about 1906 to make use of the superb bank-robbing opportunities and are said to have met their end just up the road from Tupiza in a hail of bullets. North of Tupiza in the Cinti Valley, astride the old smugglers' route from PotosÃ to Buenos Aires, I had lunch at San Pedro, which, having been founded in the 16th century, is one of the region's oldest vineyards. Graceful whitewashed buildings were set around the cobbled courtyards. Bougainvillea tumbled, fountains trickled, staff scurried, cooking fires blazed beneath ancient stone ovens. My guide and I were ushered into the dining room, where a long table was set with silver cutlery, delicate porcelain, and a bewildering array of engraved glasses. A waiter hovered. Dour portraits looked down from the walls, French windows were open to the vineyards below, and in the salon was a piano made on the rue de Rivoli in Paris. Eighty-something Lorgio Jaime Rivera Calabi held court at the head of the table, his eyes swimming in a face like parchment. He was a gracious host, given to long-winded toasts I struggled to follow. At the other end of the table was his 17-year-old daughter, Luciana, the knowledgeable heir to the estate who watched her aged father with a mixture of concern and admiration. Production at San Pedro is now focused on its famous singani, a white grape brandy and the Bolivian national drink. He poured a small glassful and explained its religious significance, how it was not just a drink but a libation. People used it to bless the dead, to pay tribute to gods, to seal an agreement. âMay you be as fortunate in your children as I have been,â he said, raising his glass. The old eyes seemed to fill. Luciana, embarrassed, looked away to the vines of muscatel beyond the French windows. The previous day I had been with GermÃ¡n Villamor, who, tragically, had been less fortunate with his children. His was a more recent arrival in the world of wines. The Tierra Roja estate was created by his son, Cristian, who had struggled with the idea of the family business; Villamor owned the Bolivian equivalent of Hallmark cards. After a course in viticulture in Italy, Cristian had planted a vineyard of Cabernet in the Cinti Valley. Then suddenly, in 2016, he died of an aneurysm at the age of 37. Heartbroken, Villamor sold his business and came to the town of Villa Abecia to continue his son's work. âCristian wasn't interested in making money,â he said as he showed us around the vineyard. âHe wasn't driven by commercial instincts. But he had a passion, and I have come to run the winery to honor him.â He brought in experienced enologists to advise him and planted more vines as well as citrus fruit trees. After a few years his wines began to win prizes. One vintage was bought by Central, a Lima restaurant that's among the best in the world. He told us to always harvest Malbec grapes at night because they will hold their flavors better. And to never prune under a full moon because the cuts will weep. Leading us down the rows of vines with his walking stick, Villamor was like a pilgrim seeking solace for a battered soul. In the midst of the vines, he stopped by a headstone, his son's grave. âEven if you don't see me or feel me, I am by your side,â the inscription read. âWe make a wine called Hummingbird,â said Villamor. âSometimes when I hear the birds hum, I feel it is my son speaking to me, saying he is happy with my work here. My son's death gave me a new life. I want Cristian to be proud of me.â He stretched his arms to encompass the vineyard, the verdant valley, the wide sky. âLife here is beautiful,â he said, smiling. âI am so grateful to him.â I found my soul's solace at the San Francisco de la Horca winery. Its owner, Marcelo Vacaflores RamÃrez, is a slight man in his 60s with a mischievous, elfin air. He showed us around his bodega, full of equipment assembled in another age: oak barrels, huge earthen pots whose clay lent a particular flavor to his wine. The whole place marinated in the rich, musty odor of fermenting grapes. âWe are four generations here,â he said. âI was born here. I am like one of the old cepas de uvaâthe grape vines.â In the courtyard of the house, we sat under the shade of the loggia while RamÃrez talked about the different wines and vintages as if they were personalities, close friends whom he was keen we should know and like. He appeared from the depths of the old house with platters of goat cheese and cured meats. He gleefully opened bottles (the labels handwritten; the corks sealed with beeswax) and poured wine, then more. There was a big Burgundy-style red made from the Negra Criolla grape and a wonderful Muscat of Alexandria white. I began to lose track. We had been traveling for several days, and now we were becalmed in this sylvan paradise, behind a high garden wall, among fragrant lavender bushes and the sound of birdsong. The glasses of wine kept arriving and I felt I never wanted to leave. The afternoon light filtered down through the yellow-flowering jacaranda trees. We tried the singani, treating it with due respect. This was followed by an exquisite cognac-style drink. We rounded off our tasting with an astonishing pomegranate liqueur. I was lifted from my seat reluctantly as the guide helped me into the car. In PotosÃ we stepped from passion to greed. Dating from 1545, PotosÃ owes its existence to a single and singular pyramid-shaped mountain that looms above the city streets. Cerro Rico, or Rich Mountain, was the world's most profitable source of silver. Carried across the ocean in galleons, dodging storms and English pirates (Francis Drake was said to have plundered about $600 million worth of silver in today's money), it made the Spanish monarchs the wealthiest in Europe. It was the silver used to mint Spanish dollars, or pieces of eight, the world's first international currency. It funded wars against the English, the Dutch, and the French. It is thought to have caused rampant inflation across Europe and sparked a global trade in luxury goods such as Chinese porcelain and Indian textiles. In PotosÃ it financed the grandiose palaces and churches that line the narrow streets. Greed is in the very mortar of the buildingsâexaggerated and self-important. In the basement of the colossal Casa Nacional de la Moneda, the national mint, I found the smelting rooms where enslaved Africans worked the furnaces in inhumane temperatures. The guide described how these poor souls never survived longer than six months. Cerro Rico still towers over the rooftops. And silver, tin, and zinc continue to be mined here. In the course of yielding about 66,000 tons of silver, the mountain has also sent an estimated 9 million men to an early grave, the victims of silicosis, toxic gases, mercury poisoning, tunnel collapses, dynamite accidents, and sheer exhaustion. Local guides say that as many as 20,000 men still work in the mine in conditions that have hardly changed since the 16th century. We had arranged to go inside, with a former miner acting as our tour guide. On our way to the mountain, we stopped to buy obligatory gifts for the workers: coca leaves, black cigarettes, a bottle of pure cane alcohol that was 96 percent ABV, and sticks of dynamite. Kitted up in overalls, helmets, and rubber boots, we climbed to an entrance tunnel, above which llama blood had been smeared across the rock face. We followed the guide inside, stooping to avoid banging our heads on the low ceiling. Behind us the circle of daylight at the entrance grew smaller and smaller as we stumbled along the tunnel. Suddenly there was a loud rattling, and the lights of head torches danced upon the walls ahead. We pressed against the tunnel wall as an ore cart clattered past on tracks. Coming up from the bowels of the mountain, two grimy miners, their faces running with sweat, were pushing the cart. Then there was darkness, and we fumbled with our torches to see where we were going. Cerro Rico felt like the depths of hell. I loved it. There was a devil in this hell. His name is El TÃo, The Uncle. We found him just beyond the point where the last ray of daylight could be seen. In a side alcove squatted a strange mannequin, covered in coca leaves and colored ribbons, sporting a huge erect phallus and a leering smile. This demonic figure, considered the Lord of the Mountain, presides over the mine. To keep the miners safe, he requires tribute. Bottles were piled by his feet as gifts. I spotted one of San Pedro singani. Packets of cigarettes had been stuffed into his stumpy hands. The sacrificial llama blood smeared above the entrance was a way to assuage his lust for blood that otherwise might only be satisfied by the death of a miner. From PotosÃ we drove west across the high plateau framed by russet hills, past llamas and vicuÃ±as grazing on tough grasses. Aloof and superior, they turned their heads to watch us, pursing their lips and batting long eyelashes. As we rose over the shoulder of a mountain dusted with green shrubs, we looked down from the pass onto a vast plain. Below was a great expanse of white, like a shining sea: the Salar de Uyuni, Bolivia's most famous salt flat. At more than 4,000 square miles, it is less than half the size of New Jersey. It's said that Neil Armstrong could see it from space. The silhouettes of dark mountains stood around its white rim. My base in this moonscape was a new upscale lodge, Jirira, created by high-end Chilean tour operator Explora, which takes clients on La TravesÃa: a bespoke journey between its sharply designed properties. From Jirira, visitors can travel across volcano ranges to the Ramaditas and Chituca lodges in Bolivia, and over the border to Explora Atacama in the Chilean desert. Until now accommodations on our wanderings had been rambling atmospheric estanciasâold-fashioned colonial properties with courtyardsâwith rooms the size of squash courts decorated with charming antiques. Special mention goes to Hotel Museo Cayara, one of the oldest Spanish houses in South America, close to PotosÃ. Built in 1557, it has many portraits of Iberian monarchs, along with muskets, dueling pistols, armor with a dented breast plate, and a library of priceless 17th-century books bound in goatskin, including a daunting 61-volume set of Voltaire. The stories of the house were like a child's book of adventures. Marquises came and went, marriages were arranged, wars raged, silver was discovered. I prowled through the back rooms, hoping to find a cupboard where sacks full of pieces of eight were hidden. Explora Jirira Lodge, however, was on another level. At first glance the building, sitting on a ridge above the flats, seemed to consist of three long shipping containers, curiously suited to this angular landscape. Designed by Chilean architect Max NÃºÃ±ez, the prefabricated modular structures were installed on stilts to have minimal impact and to allow them to be removed and repurposed. Inside, the industrial feel fell away. The interiors have an elegant simplicity, all space and light; the walls are lined with Bolivian wood, the pale furnishings are deep and inviting, the artwork reflects the flora and fauna. There is an open kitchen and two long tables for communal dinners. Designed by Mauricio LÃ³pez and SebastiÃ¡n GimÃ©nez, of hit La Paz restaurant Ancestral, the menus are proudly Bolivian, using the country's fabulous ingredients, cooked and served by locals. The lodge is one of the finest properties in Bolivia. Few places on earth are as astonishing as the Salar de Uyuni. With a fine-gravel-like surface, its far-reaching expanses glitter and sparkle. In the morning I woke to see just beneath my room flocks of flamingos, which live on the mineral marsh on the edge of the salt flats, and waited for them to rise as one and sail away, a wave of pink. We climbed K'ajchi Island, a small volcano that erupted from the seabed when the salt flats were ocean, its slopes teeming with white butterflies and strange cacti on whose flowers giant hummingbirds fed. We drove to the high shoulders of Tunupa volcano, where locals had piled cairns in tribute to the apu, or mountain spirits. Its half-collapsed cone was a riot of mineral color: red iron, yellow sulfur, and white sodium set among protrusions of black basalt. At night, brilliant constellations swarmed across the sky with such clarity I felt they might cascade down across my bed. For much of the year, stretches of the salt flats are covered in a couple of inches of water, creating a canvas of reflections. As I walked out into this mirrored world, the only things that moved were the reflections of the clouds, slowly drifting past, ravelling and unraveling around my feet. Without the usual prompts to assess scale, all sense of perspective was lost. There was no way to measure size or distance. It was a vast and peaceful nothingness. In this white void the stillness and silence were profound. The landscape of the salar, with mountains ghosting around the horizons on their reversed images, became a meditation. It was humbling. It offered the welcome gift of making me feel insignificant. And nothing is quite so good for the soul. Dehouche can arrange an 11-night Bolivian trip covering Santa Cruz de la Sierra, the wine region, PotosÃ, the salt flats, and La Paz, with all-inclusive accommodations and flights, from $17,740 per person. This article appeared in the November 2026 issue of CondÃ© Nast Traveler. Subscribe to the magazine here.

item.title: 'Changed My Life' Lentil Soup and More Recipes We Made This Week
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Itâs no secret that Bon AppÃ©tit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes weâre whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here. A fried fish sandwich has no season. Also, Iâm currently in Tennessee, where itâs hit 90Â° this week, so itâs basically still summer. I used my colleague Shilpa Uskokovicâs excellent Fritto Misto batter to coat some flounder. After frying, I slid a couple small fillets into top-split hot dog buns with juicy slices of tomato and a quick tartar sauce. It was pure summer satisfaction, even this deep into October. âJoe Sevier, senior editor, SEO and cooking We are squarely back in school and with that comes snack requests. The Gourmet stalwart, Chocolate Chip Cookies, remains a reliable favorite in our household. I know this is a hit because itâs the one requested by not just my own child, but her hungry friends. The 2026 update has me sprinkling just a touch of flaky salt on top of each one. âHana Asbrink, deputy food editor The days when my husband and I both commute are, to put it lightly, b-a-n-a-n-a-s. Thatâs when my deep freezer fulfills its destiny. Case in point: this superlative basil pesto, thawed overnight, tossed with hot rigatoni, plus frozen peas thrown in with the pasta for the last few minutes of boiling. It is nourishing and feels purposeful, even if it took less than 10 minutes of effort. âEmma Laperruque, cooking director Andy Baraghaniâs Honey-Chipotle Shrimp Tacos are one of my most-made recipes of all time. Last week I decided to change things up and eat the shrimp over some homemade Mexican rice and beans instead of wrapping them in a tortilla. The shrimp are so easy to make (just toss in a two-ingredient marinade and pan-fry) that I ended up cooking fresh batches for lunch on the following days to pair with the leftover rice and beans. The canned chipotles in adobo lend a smoky complexity, and I love how the honey helps the shrimp take on just enough char. A luxurious WFH lunch if there ever was one! âAlaina Chou, commerce writer Soup on a weeknight? Itâs a foreign concept to me. If Iâm making soup, Iâm committing hours to the cause. But this week I couldnât quell my craving for a sippable bowl, so I scoured the archive for a quick hit and landed on this Curried Lentil, Tomato, and Coconut Soup. Red lentils break down and create a substantial body, while golden Japanese S&B curry powder adds a mellow earthy kick. After mixing in crushed tomatoes and coconut milk, I went rogue and followed up with a couple dashes of fish sauce for extra umami. âNina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking The ever adaptable rotisserie chicken is one of my favorite emergency dinners. When crunched for time, Iâll grab one on my way home and transform the bird into something unrecognizable. Most recently, I used it to make Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkserâs Nuoc Cham Chicken Salad. The pulled meat is tossed with the quickest mayo-lime dressing, then stuffed into lettuce leaves. I like to finish the cups with sliced cucumber, fried shallots, and a flurry of fresh herbs. Donât bother bringing out plates. I eat this with my hands straight from the platter like nachos. âCarly Westerfield, manager, audience strategy Whenever I want something more for breakfast, but I donât want to work for it, itâs a Dutch baby all the way. Heat a skillet with butter, dump a couple of always-on-hand ingredientsâeggs, flour, milk, sugarâinto a blender, and 20 minutes later, it isnât breakfast: Itâs brunch. Last weekend I tossed the reserved browned butter from Epiâs Take It Easy Dutch Baby into a bowl of sliced Italian plums. I added a glug of maple syrup and a pinch of salt, then let the fruit soak in the flavors while I fiddled over my coffee. Puffed bÃ©bÃ© out of the oven, the plums and all their juices went on top, and I sat down to enjoy my morning. âJoe Sevier, senior editor, cooking and SEO I make lentil soup pretty frequently once the âfeels likeâ temperature dips below 50 degrees. And I was just about to mince up my mirepoix when I stumbled upon senior Test Kitchen editor Shilpa Uskokovicâs Soy-Braised Black Lentils. The promise of salty, tender-but-toothsome legumes on a bed of rice was good enough to shake up my routine. I hauled out my rice cooker, set it to steam, and started a dead-simple simmer of a pack of shiny black Beluga lentils with glugs of soy sauce and thin slices of garlic. Once the liquid was mostly gone, I stirred in glossy agave nectar plus added sugar until they formed a loose, syrupy glaze. We ate half the pot tucked into sheets of toasted seaweed snack along with generous spoonfuls of rice. The next morning, the rest was eaten with crusty bread and fried eggs. âKelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor Ever since I started working at BA, Iâve seen this single recipe for Bolognese top the charts time and time again. An oldie but a baddie, itâs received over 500 comments that would taunt me on a daily basis, with one overall glaring thesis: Make this! Now! So I decided to hunker down, put on a killer album (Once in a Lifetime), and get comfortable in the kitchen. Yes, this Bolognese takes timeâcough cough, three hoursâbut so do all good things. For those who need immediate gratification, your kitchen will be awash in the savory, primal smells of browned beef and pancetta in just 10 minutes. After adding a good amount of liquid from wine, stock, and milk (in stages), then stirring, dancing, and stirring, it was finally time to serve my meaty sauce tangled with fat pappardelle and a charitable shower of Parmesan. âNina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking When I saw a bunch of bright-eyed leeks at the farmers market from my favorite vendor, I knew just what to do with them: my colleague Rebecca Firkserâs cheesy baked pasta. It was one of those love-at-first-sight recipes for me in the Test Kitchenâsomehow minimalist and dramatic at the same time. Save this one for a chilly night when youâre having friends over. The sauce uses a cup of white wine, so thereâs most of a bottle left to enjoy with dinner. âEmma Laperruque, cooking director Iâve been making a lot of solo dinners lately, and nine times out of ten that means Iâm cooking an omelet. My version with fried shallot, apple, and Fontina cheese is a go-toâI wrote all about it for our series, Me, Myself, and Dinnerâbut if I havenât gone grocery shopping, Iâll just cobble together fun stuff from my fridge. Some recent wins: chopped kimchi and yellow cheddar; spinach, feta, and dill; black beans, avocado, and salsa macha. âRebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor This week I did something I havenât done in years. I roasted a chicken. And it was revelatory. Not fussy. Easy! Rewarding. Inspired by the method in Kitty Cowlesâs cookbook, I sprinkled the bird with salt and let it hang out in the fridge for a few hours. Then I rubbed it with olive oil, threw some lemon and garlic in the cavity, and roasted it as high as my oven would go, convection on. While the chicken was resting, its skin a golden crackle, I deglazed the pan juices with white wine, and let those simmer into a tangy gravy. Served with a salad, it was the coziest supper, even romantic if you ignore my toddler cooing. The next day, the carcass simmered in a pot of water with onion and ginger for a broth Iâll sip for days. The surplus meat has morphed into a rice bowl, towering sandwich, day care lunch box, 3 p.m. snack. And the joy from it all? Incalculable. âE.L. Iâm always on the hunt for a protein-rich, not-too-finicky dinner that I can pull together in a blip. Itâs gotta taste good because Iâll probably cook it for five consecutive days, at which point I will tire of it and resume my hunt anew. Like sands through the hourglass, these are the recipes of our lives. This week I settled on customizable Soy-Glazed Salmon Bowls. Cook the salmon in that salty-sweet soy and honey sauce, throw it atop rice, and add whatever vegetables you have. This time, I went with shreddy carrots and cukes, plus some of those crispy sheets of nori that I used to scoop up bite after bite. âSam Stone, senior editor My very talented colleague Shilpa Uskokovic forever changed the way I cook ground chicken. She mixes the chicken with baking sodaâyes, baking sodaâfor clusters of bouncy nubbins. Now, anytime a recipe calls for ground meat, I use this hack. This weekâs victim: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps. It has a sweet, fiery sauce made from sriracha, brown sugar, soy, and fish sauce that deliberately clings to the juicy meat. I piled the chicken into butter lettuce with a squeeze of lime, and a handful of torn mint for freshness. âNina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

item.title: If a Silent Retreat Is Too Much, Ease Into the Trend With a Silent Dinner
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
The awkwardness settled over the room almost immediately, heavy enough to suppress the uncomfortable smile tugging at my cheeks as I looked around from stranger to stranger. I had, after all, signed up for a seat at this 90-minute, five-course meditative meal with 16 people Iâd never met, and had agreed to do it all without sharing a single word. But knowing youâre about to break bread in absolute silence and actually finding yourself seated at a rectangular table that looked vaguely reminiscent of a Game of Thrones feast, with the sounds of forks scraping plates, throats being cleared, the seconds ticking by on the wall clockâand most importantly, nothing elseâare two very different things. While this might sound like torture to some people, all 16 of us had willingly volunteered to participate in Rancho La Puertaâs iconic Silent Dinner, a complimentary event the wellness hotel has been hosting for at least 15 years. And weâre not the only ones intrigued by the idea of adding quiet experiences into our vacations. Hilton's 2026 Trends Report identified âhushpitalityâ as one of the year's emerging travel trends, highlighting a growing desire among travelers to seek out destinations and experiences that help turn down the noise of everyday life and embrace moments of quiet. At the Ranch, that philosophy has long been woven into the guest experience, from onsite labyrinths and silent meditation sessions to sunrise mountain hikes, all free of man-made noise. In our small private indoor dining room in the mountainous countryside of Tecate, Baja California, the absence of noise wasnât simply the backdrop to dinner; it was the main course. Once our guide rang the bell, the rules of the evening were officially in effect. To request something from our waiterâmore butter, a strawâwe had to find other ways to communicate. (When I wanted an extra slice of bread, I raised my arm and mimed slicing a loaf across the palm of my hand; thanks to my incredible thespian skills, the waiter understood.) Some guests closed their eyes throughout the meal. Others ate with their hands. Phones, already highly discouraged outside of your private guest room at the Ranch, were not allowed at the dinner at all. Instead, the various knickknacks sprinkled across our communal table offered a form of entertainment. At one point, I turned to the three-eyed ceramic creature nearest me and swiveled it around so that we were watching each other, the extra company a welcome distraction from fighting my nervous laughter that was desperate to give any explosion of sound to the evening. It wasnât until the third course was whisked away, a delightful black bean soup, that I started to settle into my chair, less interested in whether my neighbor was cringing at the sound of me slurping from my spoon and more attuned to the way my mind started to pleasantly wander. As a mother with a toddler at home in New York, my life is rarely graced with stillness. Usually, I like it that way. However, in this pocket of reprieve, where nobody needed anything from me, nobody could reach me, and I had only the vantage point of my own self for 90 whole, consecutive minutes, part of me started to shift. My shoulders fell away from my ears, I breathed deeper, and the voice in my head went from rattling through my endless to-do list to something closer to reflection. Without my brain sprinting forward, I recounted a favorite line from a book Iâd read last summer that Iâd written down in my Notes app and promptly forgot entirely. A montage of images of my daughterâs childhood sauntered by, and the ending to an article I was working on simply came to me, my writerâs block annihilated so immediately that the moment felt anticlimactic. I wasnât trying to do anything in particular, I just was. And in that was-ness, silence became an opportunity to listen, make connections, and offer surprises. When the bell tolled 90 minutes later, I wasnât the only one to involuntarily jolt from my cocoon of calm. All of us stayed after to share our observations with the group. One of the women said sheâd never smiled at so many people in a room before. An older gentleman said he had pretended like he had been sharing a meal with his late wife, which prompted his neighbor to lean over and give him a hug. Our guide thanked the person next to her who helped interpret her request for salt, the two having worked together to signal the desire to the waiter. Without conversation to fill the space between us, we became more attuned to each otherâand to ourselves. Silence, it turned out, wasnât isolating us; it was offering us a different way to connect. As our evening concluded, nobody rushed to leave. People lingered, trading observations and phone numbers. During the dinner, we had all retreated into our own little worlds, but we left having, somehow, shared one. Other hotels where travelers can embrace the quiet: - Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise: Quiet the noise at Basin, the propertyâs thermal bathing facility, and run, do not walk, to book the transformative Aufguss experience led by the on-site sauna master. Itâs a multisensory sauna experience designed around heat, scent, breath, and ritual. Their guided silent hike around Lake Louise is another highlight. - Olympic Spa Hotel: Go for the Dolomites Sleep Retreat where the absence of noise, reduced light pollution, and pure mountain air are designed to help you improve your natural sleep cycle. - Eremito: At this contemporary hermitage in the Umbrian countryside, there is no Wi-Fi, television, or mobile signal in the rooms. Instead, the experience is built around reading, nature, reflection, andâperhaps most radicallyânothing in particular.
